case_info.scenario: A 13-year-old boy with an unsteady gait was referred for evaluation. He had been well until 1 month prior, when he developed lower limb weakness after eating a vegetarian diet for 15 days. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. His walking had become unsteady, and he was less talkative. On examination, he scored 24 on a Mini-Mental State Examination, with impairments in temporal and spatial orientation, calculation, and short-term memory. Horizontal nystagmus was observed. His lower limb strength was 4 of 5 proximally and 5− of 5 distally, with increased muscle tone. Patellar reflexes were brisk. Ankle clonus and Babinski signs were present bilaterally. His gait was spastic (Video). Blood test results indicated normocytic anemia (hemoglobin level, 126 g/L; reference, >130 g/L [to convert to grams per deciliter, multiply by 0.1]), borderline folate elevation (2.15 ng/mL; reference, >2 μg/L [to convert nanomoles per liter, multiply by 2.266]), and an increased homocysteine level (8.85 mg/L; reference, <2.03 mg/L [to convert to micromoles per liter, multiply by 7.397]). Results of stool analysis; liver and kidney function tests; myocardial enzyme, electrolyte, ammonia, trace element, and B12levels; thyroid function, arterial blood gas, antinuclear antibodies, and intrinsic factor antibody tests; and an infection panel test were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging showed mild cerebral atrophy and a hyperintense T2-weighted signal in the cervical spinal cord. Electromyography results were normal. Electroencephalography showed diffuse background slowing with scattered epileptiform discharges. Urine organic acid analysis indicated methylmalonic acidemia. A serum amino acid analysis was nondiagnostic (Figure 1). Cerebrospinal fluid was normal.

case_info.explanation: This teenager presented with subacute-onset spastic gait and homocysteine elevation. Homocysteinemia can be acquired or inherited with or without methylmalonic acidemia. His age, normal vitamin and folate levels, and lack of intrinsic factor antibodies suggested an inherited metabolic disorder. Elevation of methylmalonic acid (MMA) narrowed the differential diagnosis. Methylmalonic acidemia with homocysteinemia is caused by defects in the absorption, transportation, and metabolism of cobalamin.1Normally, after entering the cell, cobalamin is reduced to cobalamin II through functions of cobalamin F, J, C, and D. Next, cobalamin II is converted to methyl-cobalamin, remethylating homocysteine to methionine. Alternatively, cobalamin II can be converted to adenosyl-cobalamin, a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which converts L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. Blocking this step results in accumulation of L-methylmalonyl-CoA metabolites, which include MMA and methyl citrate acid. Therefore, any defect affecting conversion of cobalamin to cobalamin II will cause simultaneous elevations in homocysteine and MMA, leading to neuronal and endothelial dysfunctions. A cobalamin C (CblC) deficiency (choice B) is most likely. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (choice A) can present with spastic gait, encephalopathy, and seizure but cannot explain the abnormal biochemical results. Cystathionine β-synthase and methionine synthase catalyze conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine and methionine, respectively. Although defects in cystathionine β-synthase (choice C) or cobalamin G or methionine synthase (choice D) can cause homocysteinemia, neither leads to elevated MMA because adenosylcobalamin is unaffected. Whole-exome genetic sequencing revealed compound heterozygous variations (exon 4: p.Arg161Gln; p.Trp203Ter) in the patient’sMMACHCgene, confirming late-onset CblC deficiency. Folate, methyl-cobalamin, and levocarnitine were prescribed. One month later, the homocysteine level was 4.08 mg/L and his gait had slightly improved. The slow recovery may have been because of delayed diagnosis. Deficiency in CblC is autosomal recessive. It is the most common intracellular cobalaminopathy, with an incidence estimated at 1 per 3920 individuals in Shandong province, China; 1 per 60 000 in California; and 1 per 37 000 in the US Hispanic population.2,3Early-onset forms typically manifest as poor feeding, lethargy, developmental delay, and microcephaly in the neonatal period. Late-onset forms present in adolescence or adulthood and are often triggered by dehydration, vegan diet, infection, or pregnancy. Clinical manifestations are heterogeneous and include encephalopathy, myelopathy, peripheral neuropathy, dystonia, ataxia, gait abnormality, thromboembolic events, cytopenia, chronic kidney disease, and optic nerve atrophy. Severity varies from no symptoms to multisystemic involvement.4Neuroradiological features are nonspecific and may include cerebral atrophy, edema, leukoencephalopathy, infarction, corpus callosum thinning, and abnormal signals in the basal ganglia region. Spinal cord imaging features may mimic subacute combined degeneration, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, and syringomyelia.5Biochemical abnormalities provide important diagnostic clues. Organic acid profiling is characterized by elevations in MMA and methyl citrate acid. Since carnitine binds acyl residues to aid the excretion of propionyl-CoA, patients may show increases in propionyl carnitine levels (>5 μmol/L) and propionyl carnitine–acetyl carnitine ratio (>0.25) (Figure 2).6Confirmatory diagnosis requires gene sequencing. Treatment is aimed at decreasing MMA levels, promoting homocysteine-to-methionine conversion, and accelerating acyl carnitine clearance. Long-term use of parenteral hydroxocobalamin, methyl-cobalamin, or betaine; folate; and L-carnitine is warranted.4Available treatments may be region-specific, and a metabolic physician should be consulted. Protein restriction is not recommended. Urine MMA and serum homocysteine levels should be monitored. Diagnosing a late-onset CblC deficiency is challenging because of its rarity and heterogeneity. This case highlights the value of screening for methylmalonic acidemia when facing spastic gait of unknown cause and importance of early treatment to avoid irreversible neurological complications.

The appropriate next diagnostic step would be to send plasma total homocysteine and urinary methylmalonic acid for quantification, as the initial results are qualitative or borderline, and to consider genetic testing for the MMACHC gene. imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.

[Cognitive Burden]

- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,

  "frustration": <integer 1-5>,

}

case_info.explanation: This teenager presented with subacute-onset spastic gait and homocysteine elevation. Homocysteinemia can be acquired or inherited with or without methylmalonic acidemia. His age, normal vitamin and folate levels, and lack of intrinsic factor antibodies suggested an inherited metabolic disorder. Elevation of methylmalonic acid (MMA) narrowed the differential diagnosis. Methylmalonic acidemia with homocysteinemia is caused by defects in the absorption, transportation, and metabolism of cobalamin.1Normally, after entering the cell, cobalamin is reduced to cobalamin II through functions of cobalamin F, J, C, and D. Next, cobalamin II is converted to methyl-cobalamin, remethylating homocysteine to methionine. Alternatively, cobalamin II can be converted to adenosyl-cobalamin, a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which converts L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. Blocking this step results in accumulation of L-methylmalonyl-CoA metabolites, which include MMA and methyl citrate acid. Therefore, any defect affecting conversion of cobalamin to cobalamin II will cause simultaneous elevations in homocysteine and MMA, leading to neuronal and endothelial dysfunctions. A cobalamin C (CblC) deficiency (choice B) is most likely. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (choice A) can present with spastic gait, encephalopathy, and seizure but cannot explain the abnormal biochemical results. Cystathionine β-synthase and methionine synthase catalyze conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine and methionine, respectively. Although defects in cystathionine β-synthase (choice C) or cobalamin G or methionine synthase (choice D) can cause homocysteinemia, neither leads to elevated MMA because adenosylcobalamin is unaffected. Whole-exome genetic sequencing revealed compound heterozygous variations (exon 4: p.Arg161Gln; p.Trp203Ter) in the patient’sMMACHCgene, confirming late-onset CblC deficiency. Folate, methyl-cobalamin, and levocarnitine were prescribed. One month later, the homocysteine level was 4.08 mg/L and his gait had slightly improved. The slow recovery may have been because of delayed diagnosis. Deficiency in CblC is autosomal recessive. It is the most common intracellular cobalaminopathy, with an incidence estimated at 1 per 3920 individuals in Shandong province, China; 1 per 60 000 in California; and 1 per 37 000 in the US Hispanic population.2,3Early-onset forms typically manifest as poor feeding, lethargy, developmental delay, and microcephaly in the neonatal period. Late-onset forms present in adolescence or adulthood and are often triggered by dehydration, vegan diet, infection, or pregnancy. Clinical manifestations are heterogeneous and include encephalopathy, myelopathy, peripheral neuropathy, dystonia, ataxia, gait abnormality, thromboembolic events, cytopenia, chronic kidney disease, and optic nerve atrophy. Severity varies from no symptoms to multisystemic involvement.4Neuroradiological features are nonspecific and may include cerebral atrophy, edema, leukoencephalopathy, infarction, corpus callosum thinning, and abnormal signals in the basal ganglia region. Spinal cord imaging features may mimic subacute combined degeneration, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, and syringomyelia.5Biochemical abnormalities provide important diagnostic clues. Organic acid profiling is characterized by elevations in MMA and methyl citrate acid. Since carnitine binds acyl residues to aid the excretion of propionyl-CoA, patients may show increases in propionyl carnitine levels (>5 μmol/L) and propionyl carnitine–acetyl carnitine ratio (>0.25) (Figure 2).6Confirmatory diagnosis requires gene sequencing. Treatment is aimed at decreasing MMA levels, promoting homocysteine-to-methionine conversion, and accelerating acyl carnitine clearance. Long-term use of parenteral hydroxocobalamin, methyl-cobalamin, or betaine; folate; and L-carnitine is warranted.4Available treatments may be region-specific, and a metabolic physician should be consulted. Protein restriction is not recommended. Urine MMA and serum homocysteine levels should be monitored. Diagnosing a late-onset CblC deficiency is challenging because of its rarity and heterogeneity. This case highlights the value of screening for methylmalonic acidemia when facing spastic gait of unknown cause and importance of early treatment to avoid irreversible neurological complications.

1. Mental Demand

   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."

       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how

3. Effort

   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.

     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"

       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"

case_info.explanation: This teenager presented with subacute-onset spastic gait and homocysteine elevation. Homocysteinemia can be acquired or inherited with or without methylmalonic acidemia. His age, normal vitamin and folate levels, and lack of intrinsic factor antibodies suggested an inherited metabolic disorder. Elevation of methylmalonic acid (MMA) narrowed the differential diagnosis. Methylmalonic acidemia with homocysteinemia is caused by defects in the absorption, transportation, and metabolism of cobalamin.1Normally, after entering the cell, cobalamin is reduced to cobalamin II through functions of cobalamin F, J, C, and D. Next, cobalamin II is converted to methyl-cobalamin, remethylating homocysteine to methionine. Alternatively, cobalamin II can be converted to adenosyl-cobalamin, a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which converts L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. Blocking this step results in accumulation of L-methylmalonyl-CoA metabolites, which include MMA and methyl citrate acid. Therefore, any defect affecting conversion of cobalamin to cobalamin II will cause simultaneous elevations in homocysteine and MMA, leading to neuronal and endothelial dysfunctions. A cobalamin C (CblC) deficiency (choice B) is most likely. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (choice A) can present with spastic gait, encephalopathy, and seizure but cannot explain the abnormal biochemical results. Cystathionine β-synthase and methionine synthase catalyze conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine and methionine, respectively. Although defects in cystathionine β-synthase (choice C) or cobalamin G or methionine synthase (choice D) can cause homocysteinemia, neither leads to elevated MMA because adenosylcobalamin is unaffected. Whole-exome genetic sequencing revealed compound heterozygous variations (exon 4: p.Arg161Gln; p.Trp203Ter) in the patient’sMMACHCgene, confirming late-onset CblC deficiency. Folate, methyl-cobalamin, and levocarnitine were prescribed. One month later, the homocysteine level was 4.08 mg/L and his gait had slightly improved. The slow recovery may have been because of delayed diagnosis. Deficiency in CblC is autosomal recessive. It is the most common intracellular cobalaminopathy, with an incidence estimated at 1 per 3920 individuals in Shandong province, China; 1 per 60 000 in California; and 1 per 37 000 in the US Hispanic population.2,3Early-onset forms typically manifest as poor feeding, lethargy, developmental delay, and microcephaly in the neonatal period. Late-onset forms present in adolescence or adulthood and are often triggered by dehydration, vegan diet, infection, or pregnancy. Clinical manifestations are heterogeneous and include encephalopathy, myelopathy, peripheral neuropathy, dystonia, ataxia, gait abnormality, thromboembolic events, cytopenia, chronic kidney disease, and optic nerve atrophy. Severity varies from no symptoms to multisystemic involvement.4Neuroradiological features are nonspecific and may include cerebral atrophy, edema, leukoencephalopathy, infarction, corpus callosum thinning, and abnormal signals in the basal ganglia region. Spinal cord imaging features may mimic subacute combined degeneration, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, and syringomyelia.5Biochemical abnormalities provide important diagnostic clues. Organic acid profiling is characterized by elevations in MMA and methyl citrate acid. Since carnitine binds acyl residues to aid the excretion of propionyl-CoA, patients may show increases in propionyl carnitine levels (>5 μmol/L) and propionyl carnitine–acetyl carnitine ratio (>0.25) (Figure 2).6Confirmatory diagnosis requires gene sequencing. Treatment is aimed at decreasing MMA levels, promoting homocysteine-to-methionine conversion, and accelerating acyl carnitine clearance. Long-term use of parenteral hydroxocobalamin, methyl-cobalamin, or betaine; folate; and L-carnitine is warranted.4Available treatments may be region-specific, and a metabolic physician should be consulted. Protein restriction is not recommended. Urine MMA and serum homocysteine levels should be monitored. Diagnosing a late-onset CblC deficiency is challenging because of its rarity and heterogeneity. This case highlights the value of screening for methylmalonic acidemia when facing spastic gait of unknown cause and importance of early treatment to avoid irreversible neurological complications.

case_info.explanation: This teenager presented with subacute-onset spastic gait and homocysteine elevation. Homocysteinemia can be acquired or inherited with or without methylmalonic acidemia. His age, normal vitamin and folate levels, and lack of intrinsic factor antibodies suggested an inherited metabolic disorder. Elevation of methylmalonic acid (MMA) narrowed the differential diagnosis. Methylmalonic acidemia with homocysteinemia is caused by defects in the absorption, transportation, and metabolism of cobalamin.1Normally, after entering the cell, cobalamin is reduced to cobalamin II through functions of cobalamin F, J, C, and D. Alternatively, cobalamin II can be converted to adenosyl-cobalamin, a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which converts L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. Blocking this step results in accumulation of L-methylmalonyl-CoA metabolites, which include MMA and methyl citrate acid. Therefore, any defect affecting conversion of cobalamin to cobalamin II will cause simultaneous elevations in homocysteine and MMA, leading to neuronal and endothelial dysfunctions. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (choice A) can present with spastic gait, encephalopathy, and seizure but cannot explain the abnormal biochemical results. Cystathionine β-synthase and methionine synthase catalyze conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine and methionine, respectively. Organic acid profiling is characterized by elevations in MMA and methyl citrate acid. Treatment is aimed at decreasing MMA levels, promoting homocysteine-to-methionine conversion, and accelerating acyl carnitine clearance. Long-term use of parenteral hydroxocobalamin, methyl-cobalamin, or betaine; folate; and L-carnitine is warranted.4Available treatments may be region-specific, and a metabolic physician should be consulted. Protein restriction is not recommended. Urine MMA and serum homocysteine levels should be monitored. Diagnosing a late-onset CblC deficiency is challenging because of its rarity and heterogeneity. This case highlights the value of screening for methylmalonic acidemia when facing spastic gait of unknown cause and importance of early treatment to avoid irreversible neurological complications.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 13-year-old boy with an unsteady gait was referred for evaluation. He had been well until 1 month prior, when he developed lower limb weakness after eating a vegetarian diet for 15 days. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. His walking had become unsteady, and he was less talkative. On examination, he scored 24 on a Mini-Mental State Examination, with impairments in temporal and spatial orientation, calculation, and short-term memory. Horizontal nystagmus was observed. His lower limb strength was 4 of 5 proximally and 5− of 5 distally, with increased muscle tone. Patellar reflexes were brisk. Ankle clonus and Babinski signs were present bilaterally. His gait was spastic (Video). Blood test results indicated normocytic anemia (hemoglobin level, 126 g/L; reference, >130 g/L [to convert to grams per deciliter, multiply by 0.1]), borderline folate elevation (2.15 ng/mL; reference, >2 μg/L [to convert nanomoles per liter, multiply by 2.266]), and an increased homocysteine level (8.85 mg/L; reference, <2.03 mg/L [to convert to micromoles per liter, multiply by 7.397]). Results of stool analysis; liver and kidney function tests; myocardial enzyme, electrolyte, ammonia, trace element, and B12levels; thyroid function, arterial blood gas, antinuclear antibodies, and intrinsic factor antibody tests; and an infection panel test were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging showed mild cerebral atrophy and a hyperintense T2-weighted signal in the cervical spinal cord. Electromyography results were normal. Electroencephalography showed diffuse background slowing with scattered epileptiform discharges. Urine organic acid analysis indicated methylmalonic acidemia. A serum amino acid analysis was nondiagnostic (Figure 1). Cerebrospinal fluid was normal.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]

{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the

}

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 5.2. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:

case_info.caption: Urine organic acid analysis using the gas chromatography–mass spectrometry method revealed increased methylmalonic acid levels in the patient sample (A) vs a normal control (B). cps indicates counts per second.
case_info.explanation: This teenager presented with subacute-onset spastic gait and homocysteine elevation. Homocysteinemia can be acquired or inherited with or without methylmalonic acidemia. His age, normal vitamin and folate levels, and lack of intrinsic factor antibodies suggested an inherited metabolic disorder. Elevation of methylmalonic acid (MMA) narrowed the differential diagnosis. Methylmalonic acidemia with homocysteinemia is caused by defects in the absorption, transportation, and metabolism of cobalamin.1Normally, after entering the cell, cobalamin is reduced to cobalamin II through functions of cobalamin F, J, C, and D. Next, cobalamin II is converted to methyl-cobalamin, remethylating homocysteine to methionine. Alternatively, cobalamin II can be converted to adenosyl-cobalamin, a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which converts L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. Blocking this step results in accumulation of L-methylmalonyl-CoA metabolites, which include MMA and methyl citrate acid. Therefore, any defect affecting conversion of cobalamin to cobalamin II will cause simultaneous elevations in homocysteine and MMA, leading to neuronal and endothelial dysfunctions. A cobalamin C (CblC) deficiency (choice B) is most likely. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (choice A) can present with spastic gait, encephalopathy, and seizure but cannot explain the abnormal biochemical results. Cystathionine β-synthase and methionine synthase catalyze conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine and methionine, respectively. Although defects in cystathionine β-synthase (choice C) or cobalamin G or methionine synthase (choice D) can cause homocysteinemia, neither leads to elevated MMA because adenosylcobalamin is unaffected. Whole-exome genetic sequencing revealed compound heterozygous variations (exon 4: p.Arg161Gln; p.Trp203Ter) in the patient’sMMACHCgene, confirming late-onset CblC deficiency. Folate, methyl-cobalamin, and levocarnitine were prescribed. One month later, the homocysteine level was 4.08 mg/L and his gait had slightly improved. The slow recovery may have been because of delayed diagnosis. Deficiency in CblC is autosomal recessive. It is the most common intracellular cobalaminopathy, with an incidence estimated at 1 per 3920 individuals in Shandong province, China; 1 per 60 000 in California; and 1 per 37 000 in the US Hispanic population.2,3Early-onset forms typically manifest as poor feeding, lethargy, developmental delay, and microcephaly in the neonatal period. Late-onset forms present in adolescence or adulthood and are often triggered by dehydration, vegan diet, infection, or pregnancy. Clinical manifestations are heterogeneous and include encephalopathy, myelopathy, peripheral neuropathy, dystonia, ataxia, gait abnormality, thromboembolic events, cytopenia, chronic kidney disease, and optic nerve atrophy. Severity varies from no symptoms to multisystemic involvement.4Neuroradiological features are nonspecific and may include cerebral atrophy, edema, leukoencephalopathy, infarction, corpus callosum thinning, and abnormal signals in the basal ganglia region. Spinal cord imaging features may mimic subacute combined degeneration, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, and syringomyelia.5Biochemical abnormalities provide important diagnostic clues. Organic acid profiling is characterized by elevations in MMA and methyl citrate acid. Since carnitine binds acyl residues to aid the excretion of propionyl-CoA, patients may show increases in propionyl carnitine levels (>5 μmol/L) and propionyl carnitine–acetyl carnitine ratio (>0.25) (Figure 2).6Confirmatory diagnosis requires gene sequencing. Treatment is aimed at decreasing MMA levels, promoting homocysteine-to-methionine conversion, and accelerating acyl carnitine clearance. Long-term use of parenteral hydroxocobalamin, methyl-cobalamin, or betaine; folate; and L-carnitine is warranted.4Available treatments may be region-specific, and a metabolic physician should be consulted. Protein restriction is not recommended. Urine MMA and serum homocysteine levels should be monitored. Diagnosing a late-onset CblC deficiency is challenging because of its rarity and heterogeneity. This case highlights the value of screening for methylmalonic acidemia when facing spastic gait of unknown cause and importance of early treatment to avoid irreversible neurological complications.

case_info.explanation: This teenager presented with subacute-onset spastic gait and homocysteine elevation. Homocysteinemia can be acquired or inherited with or without methylmalonic acidemia. His age, normal vitamin and folate levels, and lack of intrinsic factor antibodies suggested an inherited metabolic disorder. Elevation of methylmalonic acid (MMA) narrowed the differential diagnosis. Methylmalonic acidemia with homocysteinemia is caused by defects in the absorption, transportation, and metabolism of cobalamin.1Normally, after entering the cell, cobalamin is reduced to cobalamin II through functions of cobalamin F, J, C, and D. Next, cobalamin II is converted to methyl-cobalamin, remethylating homocysteine to methionine. Alternatively, cobalamin II can be converted to adenosyl-cobalamin, a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which converts L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. Blocking this step results in accumulation of L-methylmalonyl-CoA metabolites, which include MMA and methyl citrate acid. Therefore, any defect affecting conversion of cobalamin to cobalamin II will cause simultaneous elevations in homocysteine and MMA, leading to neuronal and endothelial dysfunctions. A cobalamin C (CblC) deficiency (choice B) is most likely. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (choice A) can present with spastic gait, encephalopathy, and seizure but cannot explain the abnormal biochemical results. Cystathionine β-synthase and methionine synthase catalyze conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine and methionine, respectively. Although defects in cystathionine β-synthase (choice C) or cobalamin G or methionine synthase (choice D) can cause homocysteinemia, neither leads to elevated MMA because adenosylcobalamin is unaffected. Whole-exome genetic sequencing revealed compound heterozygous variations (exon 4: p.Arg161Gln; p.Trp203Ter) in the patient’sMMACHCgene, confirming late-onset CblC deficiency. Folate, methyl-cobalamin, and levocarnitine were prescribed. One month later, the homocysteine level was 4.08 mg/L and his gait had slightly improved. The slow recovery may have been because of delayed diagnosis. Deficiency in CblC is autosomal recessive. It is the most common intracellular cobalaminopathy, with an incidence estimated at 1 per 3920 individuals in Shandong province, China; 1 per 60 000 in California; and 1 per 37 000 in the US Hispanic population.2,3Early-onset forms typically manifest as poor feeding, lethargy, developmental delay, and microcephaly in the neonatal period. Late-onset forms present in adolescence or adulthood and are often triggered by dehydration, vegan diet, infection, or pregnancy. Clinical manifestations are heterogeneous and include encephalopathy, myelopathy, peripheral neuropathy, dystonia, ataxia, gait abnormality, thromboembolic events, cytopenia, chronic kidney disease, and optic nerve atrophy. Severity varies from no symptoms to multisystemic involvement.4Neuroradiological features are nonspecific and may include cerebral atrophy, edema, leukoencephalopathy, infarction, corpus callosum thinning, and abnormal signals in the basal ganglia region. Spinal cord imaging features may mimic subacute combined degeneration, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, and syringomyelia.5Biochemical abnormalities provide important diagnostic clues. Organic acid profiling is characterized by elevations in MMA and methyl citrate acid. Since carnitine binds acyl residues to aid the excretion of propionyl-CoA, patients may show increases in propionyl carnitine levels (>5 μmol/L) and propionyl carnitine–acetyl carnitine ratio (>0.25) (Figure 2).6Confirmatory diagnosis requires gene sequencing. Treatment is aimed at decreasing MMA levels, promoting homocysteine-to-methionine conversion, and accelerating acyl carnitine clearance. Long-term use of parenteral hydroxocobalamin, methyl-cobalamin, or betaine; folate; and L-carnitine is warranted.4Available treatments may be region-specific, and a metabolic physician should be consulted. Protein restriction is not recommended. Urine MMA and serum homocysteine levels should be monitored. Diagnosing a late-onset CblC deficiency is challenging because of its rarity and heterogeneity. This case highlights the value of screening for methylmalonic acidemia when facing spastic gait of unknown cause and importance of early treatment to avoid irreversible neurological complications.

case_info.caption: Urine organic acid analysis using the gas chromatography–mass spectrometry method revealed increased methylmalonic acid levels in the patient sample (A) vs a normal control (B). cps indicates counts per second.
case_info.explanation: This teenager presented with subacute-onset spastic gait and homocysteine elevation. Homocysteinemia can be acquired or inherited with or without methylmalonic acidemia. His age, normal vitamin and folate levels, and lack of intrinsic factor antibodies suggested an inherited metabolic disorder. Elevation of methylmalonic acid (MMA) narrowed the differential diagnosis. Methylmalonic acidemia with homocysteinemia is caused by defects in the absorption, transportation, and metabolism of cobalamin.1Normally, after entering the cell, cobalamin is reduced to cobalamin II through functions of cobalamin F, J, C, and D. Next, cobalamin II is converted to methyl-cobalamin, remethylating homocysteine to methionine. Alternatively, cobalamin II can be converted to adenosyl-cobalamin, a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which converts L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. Blocking this step results in accumulation of L-methylmalonyl-CoA metabolites, which include MMA and methyl citrate acid. Therefore, any defect affecting conversion of cobalamin to cobalamin II will cause simultaneous elevations in homocysteine and MMA, leading to neuronal and endothelial dysfunctions. A cobalamin C (CblC) deficiency (choice B) is most likely. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (choice A) can present with spastic gait, encephalopathy, and seizure but cannot explain the abnormal biochemical results. Cystathionine β-synthase and methionine synthase catalyze conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine and methionine, respectively. Although defects in cystathionine β-synthase (choice C) or cobalamin G or methionine synthase (choice D) can cause homocysteinemia, neither leads to elevated MMA because adenosylcobalamin is unaffected. Whole-exome genetic sequencing revealed compound heterozygous variations (exon 4: p.Arg161Gln; p.Trp203Ter) in the patient’sMMACHCgene, confirming late-onset CblC deficiency. Folate, methyl-cobalamin, and levocarnitine were prescribed. One month later, the homocysteine level was 4.08 mg/L and his gait had slightly improved. The slow recovery may have been because of delayed diagnosis. Deficiency in CblC is autosomal recessive. It is the most common intracellular cobalaminopathy, with an incidence estimated at 1 per 3920 individuals in Shandong province, China; 1 per 60 000 in California; and 1 per 37 000 in the US Hispanic population.2,3Early-onset forms typically manifest as poor feeding, lethargy, developmental delay, and microcephaly in the neonatal period. Late-onset forms present in adolescence or adulthood and are often triggered by dehydration, vegan diet, infection, or pregnancy. Clinical manifestations are heterogeneous and include encephalopathy, myelopathy, peripheral neuropathy, dystonia, ataxia, gait abnormality, thromboembolic events, cytopenia, chronic kidney disease, and optic nerve atrophy. Severity varies from no symptoms to multisystemic involvement.4Neuroradiological features are nonspecific and may include cerebral atrophy, edema, leukoencephalopathy, infarction, corpus callosum thinning, and abnormal signals in the basal ganglia region. Spinal cord imaging features may mimic subacute combined degeneration, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, and syringomyelia.5Biochemical abnormalities provide important diagnostic clues. Organic acid profiling is characterized by elevations in MMA and methyl citrate acid. Since carnitine binds acyl residues to aid the excretion of propionyl-CoA, patients may show increases in propionyl carnitine levels (>5 μmol/L) and propionyl carnitine–acetyl carnitine ratio (>0.25) (Figure 2).6Confirmatory diagnosis requires gene sequencing. Treatment is aimed at decreasing MMA levels, promoting homocysteine-to-methionine conversion, and accelerating acyl carnitine clearance. Long-term use of parenteral hydroxocobalamin, methyl-cobalamin, or betaine; folate; and L-carnitine is warranted.4Available treatments may be region-specific, and a metabolic physician should be consulted. Protein restriction is not recommended. Urine MMA and serum homocysteine levels should be monitored. Diagnosing a late-onset CblC deficiency is challenging because of its rarity and heterogeneity. 1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."

       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's

       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration

case_info.caption: Urine organic acid analysis using the gas chromatography–mass spectrometry method revealed increased methylmalonic acid levels in the patient sample (A) vs a normal control (B). cps indicates counts per second.
case_info.explanation: This teenager presented with subacute-onset spastic gait and homocysteine elevation. Homocysteinemia can be acquired or inherited with or without methylmalonic acidemia. His age, normal vitamin and folate levels, and lack of intrinsic factor antibodies suggested an inherited metabolic disorder. Elevation of methylmalonic acid (MMA) narrowed the differential diagnosis. Methylmalonic acidemia with homocysteinemia is caused by defects in the absorption, transportation, and metabolism of cobalamin.1Normally, after entering the cell, cobalamin is reduced to cobalamin II through functions of cobalamin F, J, C, and D. Next, cobalamin II is converted to methyl-cobalamin, remethylating homocysteine to methionine. Alternatively, cobalamin II can be converted to adenosyl-cobalamin, a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which converts L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. Blocking this step results in accumulation of L-methylmalonyl-CoA metabolites, which include MMA and methyl citrate acid. Therefore, any defect affecting conversion of cobalamin to cobalamin II will cause simultaneous elevations in homocysteine and MMA, leading to neuronal and endothelial dysfunctions. A cobalamin C (CblC) deficiency (choice B) is most likely. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (choice A) can present with spastic gait, encephalopathy, and seizure but cannot explain the abnormal biochemical results. Cystathionine β-synthase and methionine synthase catalyze conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine and methionine, respectively. Although defects in cystathionine β-synthase (choice C) or cobalamin G or methionine synthase (choice D) can cause homocysteinemia, neither leads to elevated MMA because adenosylcobalamin is unaffected. Whole-exome genetic sequencing revealed compound heterozygous variations (exon 4: p.Arg161Gln; p.Trp203Ter) in the patient’sMMACHCgene, confirming late-onset CblC deficiency. Folate, methyl-cobalamin, and levocarnitine were prescribed. One month later, the homocysteine level was 4.08 mg/L and his gait had slightly improved. The slow recovery may have been because of delayed diagnosis. Deficiency in CblC is autosomal recessive. It is the most common intracellular cobalaminopathy, with an incidence estimated at 1 per 3920 individuals in Shandong province, China; 1 per 60 000 in California; and 1 per 37 000 in the US Hispanic population.2,3Early-onset forms typically manifest as poor feeding, lethargy, developmental delay, and microcephaly in the neonatal period. Late-onset forms present in adolescence or adulthood and are often triggered by dehydration, vegan diet, infection, or pregnancy. Clinical manifestations are heterogeneous and include encephalopathy, myelopathy, peripheral neuropathy, dystonia, ataxia, gait abnormality, thromboembolic events, cytopenia, chronic kidney disease, and optic nerve atrophy. Severity varies from no symptoms to multisystemic involvement.4Neuroradiological features are nonspecific and may include cerebral atrophy, edema, leukoencephalopathy, infarction, corpus callosum thinning, and abnormal signals in the basal ganglia region. Spinal cord imaging features may mimic subacute combined degeneration, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, and syringomyelia.5Biochemical abnormalities provide important diagnostic clues. Organic acid profiling is characterized by elevations in MMA and methyl citrate acid. Since carnitine binds acyl residues to aid the excretion of propionyl-CoA, patients may show increases in propionyl carnitine levels (>5 μmol/L) and propionyl carnitine–acetyl carnitine ratio (>0.25) (Figure 2).6Confirmatory diagnosis requires gene sequencing. Treatment is aimed at decreasing MMA levels, promoting homocysteine-to-methionine conversion, and accelerating acyl carnitine clearance. Long-term use of parenteral hydroxocobalamin, methyl-cobalamin, or betaine; folate; and L-carnitine is warranted.4Available treatments may be region-specific, and a metabolic physician should be consulted. Protein restriction is not recommended. Urine MMA and serum homocysteine levels should be monitored. Diagnosing a late-onset CblC deficiency is challenging because of its rarity and heterogeneity. This case highlights the value of screening for methylmalonic acidemia when facing spastic gait of unknown cause and importance of early treatment to avoid irreversible neurological complications.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 13-year-old boy with an unsteady gait was referred for evaluation. He had been well until 1 month prior, when he developed lower limb weakness after eating a vegetarian diet for 15 days. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. His walking had become unsteady, and he was less talkative. On examination, he scored 24 on a Mini-Mental State Examination, with impairments in temporal and spatial orientation, calculation, and short-term memory. Horizontal nystagmus was observed. His lower limb strength was 4 of 5 proximally and 5− of 5 distally, with increased muscle tone. Patellar reflexes were brisk. Ankle clonus and Babinski signs were present bilaterally. His gait was spastic (Video). Blood test results indicated normocytic anemia (hemoglobin level, 126 g/L; reference, >130 g/L [to convert to grams per deciliter, multiply by 0.1]), borderline folate elevation (2.15 ng/mL; reference, >2 μg/L [to convert nanomoles per liter, multiply by 2.266]), and an increased homocysteine level (8.85 mg/L; reference, <2.03 mg/L [to convert to micromoles per liter, multiply by 7.397]). Results of stool analysis; liver and kidney function tests; myocardial enzyme, electrolyte, ammonia, trace element, and B12levels; thyroid function, arterial blood gas, antinuclear antibodies, and intrinsic factor antibody tests; and an infection panel test were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging showed mild cerebral atrophy and a hyperintense T2-weighted signal in the cervical spinal cord. Electromyography results were normal. Electroencephalography showed diffuse background slowing with scattered epileptiform discharges. Urine organic acid analysis indicated methylmalonic acidemia. A serum amino acid analysis was nondiagnostic (Figure 1). Cerebrospinal fluid was normal.

You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.
